summary.text: Sea ice is frozen seawater, and since ice is less dense than liquid water it floats, covering about 7% of Earth's surface.
Its white surface bounces the Sun's energy back to space, helping keep the planet cool, while it also insulates the ocean beneath from the air.
Satellite records show Arctic sea ice shrinking in both extent and thickness in recent decades, a trend linked to global climate change.

items.prompt: Melting sea ice exposes darker open water. Before it melted, how was that ice helping keep the planet cool?

options.label: It released cold air into the sky
It sent the Sun's energy back to space
It soaked up heat from the sea floor
It blocked warm winds from the poles

items.explain: Sea ice's white surface reflects the Sun's energy back into space, a cooling process called the albedo effect.

items.prompt: Along a polar coast, a sheet of ice is frozen solid to the shoreline and stays put in a gale. What is it called?

options.label: Drift ice
Pack ice
Fast ice
Pancake ice

items.explain: Ice attached to the shoreline is landfast ice, usually just called fast ice, as in fastened; drift ice moves with currents and winds.

items.prompt: A huge block breaks off the front of a glacier and splashes into the sea. Is that block sea ice?

options.label: No; it's an iceberg, not frozen seawater
Yes; any ice floating in the sea counts
Yes, once it has spent a winter afloat
No; sea ice only forms on lakes

items.explain: Sea ice forms when seawater freezes; icebergs are chunks of ice shelves or glaciers that calve into the ocean.

items.prompt: In midwinter the polar air is far colder than the ocean beneath a sheet of sea ice. What does the ice do between them?

options.label: It speeds up heat loss from the sea
It has no effect on the exchange
It pulls carbon dioxide into the water
It limits heat and gas moving between them

items.explain: Sea ice insulates the ocean, limiting the transfer of heat, water vapour and gases such as carbon dioxide between sea and atmosphere.

items.prompt: Tiny living things make their home inside solid-looking sea ice. Where in the ice do they live?

options.label: In salty brine channels
In pockets of fresh meltwater
Only on the snow on top
In bubbles of trapped air

items.explain: Salty brine channels within the ice give microorganisms a habitat, and they form the base of unique food webs.

items.prompt: At any one time, roughly how much of the world's ocean surface is covered by sea ice?

options.label: About 1%
About 40%
About 75%
About 12%

items.explain: Sea ice covers about 12% of the world's oceans, or about 7% of Earth's whole surface.
